{{Short description|Ring in abstract algebra}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically [[abstract algebra]], an '''Artinian ring''' (sometimes '''Artin ring''') is a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] that satisfies the [[descending chain condition]] on (one-sided) [[ideal (ring theory)|ideals]]; that is, there is no infinite descending sequence of ideals. Artinian rings are named after [[Emil Artin]], who first discovered that the descending chain condition for ideals simultaneously generalizes [[finite ring]]s and rings that are [[dimension (vector space)|finite-dimensional]] [[vector space]]s over [[field (mathematics)|fields]]. The definition of Artinian rings may be restated by interchanging the descending chain condition with an equivalent notion: the [[minimum condition]].

Precisely, a ring is '''left Artinian''' if it satisfies the descending chain condition on left ideals, '''right Artinian''' if it satisfies the descending chain condition on right ideals, and '''Artinian''' or '''two-sided Artinian''' if it is both left and right Artinian.{{sfn|Brešar|2014|p=73|ps=none}}  For [[commutative ring]]s the left and right definitions coincide, but in general they are distinct from each other.

The [[Wedderburn–Artin theorem]] characterizes every [[simple ring|simple]] Artinian ring as a [[Matrix ring|ring of matrices]] over a [[division ring]].  This implies that a simple ring is left Artinian [[if and only if]] it is right Artinian.

The same definition and terminology can be applied to [[module (mathematics)|module]]s, with ideals replaced by [[submodule]]s.

Although the descending chain condition appears dual to the [[ascending chain condition]], in rings it is in fact the stronger condition.  Specifically, a consequence of the [[Hopkins–Levitzki theorem|Akizuki–Hopkins–Levitzki theorem]] is that a left (resp. right) Artinian ring is automatically a left (resp. right) [[Noetherian ring]].  This is not true for general modules; that is, an [[Artinian module]] need not be a [[Noetherian module]].

== Examples and counterexamples ==
* An [[integral domain]] is Artinian if and only if it is a field.
* A ring with finitely many, say left, ideals is left Artinian. In particular, a [[finite ring]] (e.g., <math>\mathbb{Z}/n \mathbb{Z}</math>) is left and right Artinian.
* Let <math>k</math> be a field. Then <math>k[t]/(t^n)</math> is Artinian for every positive [[integer]] ''n''.
* Similarly, <math>k[x,y]/(x^2, y^3, xy^2) = k \oplus k\cdot x \oplus k \cdot y \oplus k\cdot xy \oplus k \cdot y^2</math> is an Artinian ring with [[maximal ideal]] <math>(x,y)</math>.
* Let <math>x</math> be an endomorphism between a finite-dimensional vector space ''V''. Then the subalgebra <math>A \subset \operatorname{End}(V)</math> generated by <math>x</math> is a commutative Artinian ring.
* If ''I'' is a [[zero ideal|nonzero]] ideal of a [[Dedekind domain]] ''A'', then <math>A/I</math> is a [[principal ideal ring|principal]] Artinian ring.{{sfn|Clark|loc=Theorem 20.11|ps=none}}
* For each <math>n \ge 1</math>, the full [[matrix ring]] <math>M_n(R)</math> over a left Artinian (resp. left Noetherian) ring ''R'' is left Artinian (resp. left Noetherian).{{sfn|Cohn|2003|loc=5.2 Exercise 11|ps=none}}

The following two are examples of non-Artinian rings.
* If ''R'' is any ring, then the [[polynomial ring]] ''R''[''x''] is not Artinian, since the ideal generated by <math>x^{n+1}</math> is (properly) contained in the ideal generated by <math>x^n</math> for all [[natural numbers]] ''n''. In contrast, if ''R'' is Noetherian so is ''R''[''x''] by the [[Hilbert basis theorem]].
* The ring of integers <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> is a Noetherian ring but is not Artinian.

== Modules over Artinian rings ==
Let ''M'' be a left module over a left Artinian ring. Then the following are equivalent ([[Hopkins' theorem]]): (i) ''M'' is [[finitely generated module|finitely generated]], (ii) ''M'' has [[finite length]] (i.e., has [[composition series]]), (iii) ''M'' is Noetherian, (iv) ''M'' is Artinian.{{sfn|Bourbaki|2012|loc=VIII, p. 7|ps=none}}

== Commutative Artinian rings ==
Let ''A'' be a commutative Noetherian ring with unity. Then the following are equivalent.
* ''A'' is Artinian.
* ''A'' is a finite [[product of rings|product]] of commutative Artinian [[local ring|local rings]].{{sfn|Atiyah|Macdonald|1969|loc=Theorems 8.7|ps=none}}
* {{nowrap|''A'' / nil(''A'')}} is a [[semisimple ring]], where nil(''A'') is the [[Nilradical of a ring|nilradical]] of ''A''.{{citation needed|date=July 2012}}
* Every finitely generated module over ''A'' has finite length. (see above)
* ''A'' has [[Krull dimension]] zero.{{sfn|Atiyah|Macdonald|1969|loc=Theorems 8.5|ps=none}} (In particular, the nilradical is the [[Jacobson radical]] since [[prime ideal]]s are maximal.)
* <math>\operatorname{Spec}A</math> is finite and discrete.
* <math>\operatorname{Spec}A</math> is discrete.{{sfn|Atiyah|Macdonald|1969|loc=Ch. 8, Exercise 2|ps=none}}

Let ''k'' be a field and ''A'' a finitely generated ''k''-[[algebra over a field|algebra]]. Then ''A'' is Artinian if and only if ''A'' is finitely generated as a ''k''-module.

An Artinian local ring is complete. A [[quotient ring|quotient]] and [[localization (commutative algebra)|localization]] of an Artinian ring is Artinian.

== Simple Artinian ring ==
One version of the [[Wedderburn–Artin theorem]] states that a [[simple ring|simple]] Artinian ring ''A'' is a matrix ring over a division ring. Indeed,{{sfn|Milnor|1971|p=144|ps=none}} let ''I'' be a minimal (nonzero) right ideal of ''A'', which exists since ''A'' is Artinian (and the rest of the proof does not use the fact that ''A'' is Artinian). Then, since <math>AI</math> is a two-sided ideal, <math>AI = A</math> since ''A'' is simple. Thus, we can choose <math>a_i \in A</math> so that <math>1 \in a_1 I + \cdots + a_k I</math>. Assume ''k'' is minimal with respect to that property. 
Now consider the map of right ''A''-modules:
: <math>\begin{cases} I^{\oplus k} \to A, \\ (y_1, \dots, y_k) \mapsto a_1y_1 + \cdots + a_k y_k \end{cases}</math>

This map is [[surjective]], since the image is a right ideal and contains ''1''. If it is not [[injective]], then, say, <math>a_1y_1 = a_2y_2 + \cdots + a_k y_k</math> with nonzero <math>y_1</math>. Then, by the minimality of ''I'', we have <math>y_1 A = I</math>. It follows:
: <math>a_1 I = a_1 y_1 A \subset a_2 I + \cdots + a_k I</math>,
which contradicts the minimality of ''k''. Hence, <math>I^{\oplus k} \simeq A</math> and thus <math>A \simeq \operatorname{End}_A(A) \simeq M_k(\operatorname{End}_A(I))</math>.
